ia-warrant-or-onsite.title: Warrant or On-Site Arrest? Always Ask
ia-warrant-or-onsite.body:
The jail someone is sitting in does NOT tell you what county the charge belongs to. Getting this wrong is one of the most common intake mistakes — and it turns into wrong quotes, missed court dates, and bond forfeitures.

## The Rule

Someone pulled over for DWI gets arrested on the spot and taken to the jail where it happened — that's an **on-site arrest**, and the charge lives where the arrest happened. But if a warrant was issued earlier — say a Dallas County warrant — and the person gets picked up in Red Oak, they'll sit in the Ellis County jail and it is **still a Dallas County charge**. Being in the Ellis County jail does not make it an Ellis County case.

## The Three Questions

On every charge, confirm with the person giving you the information:

1. **Is this a warrant or an on-site arrest?**
2. **If it's a warrant — what county is it out of?**
3. **What is the warrant number?**

That's the only way to know for sure. Online jail screens often don't show it — if you can't see an offense date on that DWI, that's your cue it may be a warrant. Ask.

## Patterns Worth Knowing

- A DWI is normally an on-site arrest.
- Assault family violence is on-site about half the time — the other half, the defendant left the scene and a warrant was issued.
- Ask yourself: was he arrested ON this charge, or was he pulled over for something small (failure to ID) and found to be hiding a stack of warrants?
- When you see big multiples, there's usually stuff all over the place — a person can be picked up on warrants from three to ten other counties at once.
- If someone is hospitalized after an incident and released from the hospital, the agency just issues a warrant — so the charge shows up later as a warrant, not an arrest.

## Get It While They're In

We cannot get this information after release — the jail won't discuss why someone WAS in custody. If anything is unclear, call back while they're still in: "I didn't get all of this information — can you tell me where that one is out of?"

warrant-types.title: Warrant Types — BF, ATGOB, FTA, IB, PV
warrant-types.body:
Any extension of a warrant has a home county somewhere — and these are the charge codes that trigger the **5% risk fee** on the Quoting Guide. You'll see them on jail screens, and you'll quote off of them, so know what each one means.

## The Risk-Fee Warrant Types

- **BF — Bond Forfeiture.** The defendant missed court and the court forfeited the bond. A bond forfeiture warrant always has a home county — find it and get the warrant number.
- **FTA — Failure to Appear.** Missed court; often charged as its own offense on top of the original case.
- **PV — Probation Violation.** A warrant out of the county supervising the probation — a "Collin County DWI PV" lives in Collin County no matter where he's picked up.
- **IB — Insufficient Bond.** In Dallas County this usually happens one of two ways: the defendant missed court but the court didn't issue a bond forfeiture, or a surety went off the bond by filing a 17.16 — by the time that filing gets back to the court, an insufficient bond warrant comes out.
- **ATGOB — Affidavit To Go Off Bond** (release of surety). Every county calls this something different — AFRS (Affidavit of Release of Surety), SOB (Surety Off Bond), and others — but it's the same thing: the surety coming off the bond.

## 17.16 vs. 17.19 — Two Ways Off a Bond

- **17.16** — filed at the **jail**, while the defendant is in custody. Filed at the book-in desk; make sure the clerk file-stamps your copy and keeps the original.
- **17.19** (Code of Criminal Procedure) — filed with the **judge**, while the defendant is OUT. It's the surety telling the court before a court date: there's a problem and we don't believe he'll appear. The judge issues a warrant. If the defendant shows up to court, he's arrested on it; if he doesn't show, the bond isn't forfeited — the filing stands.

## What To Do When You See One

When a jail screen shows something like "THEFT SOB," you know two things immediately: it has a warrant number, and it has a home county. Get both.

ia-county-right.title: Why the County Must Be Right
ia-county-right.body:
One wrong county on an intake doesn't stay one mistake — it compounds through the entire life of the bond.

## It Changes the Quote

- Bond forfeiture and the other risk-fee warrant types add 5% — you can't price the bond without knowing what it is.
- The county drives geo and transfer fees. On one case marked Ellis County that was really Dallas, the bond could have been written for original signature — saving the customer the entire transfer fee.

## It Decides Where We Watch for Court

The court team follows the case in the county YOU record. A defendant sat in a dual-county jail that books for both Johnson and Tarrant County. The intake said Tarrant, so the court team watched Tarrant for settings — and the bond forfeited out of **Johnson County**. Nobody knew to look there. Wrong county means we can't tell the customer their court date, and we won't know when they miss it.

## The Safety Nets Are Thinner Than You Think

- Posting locally, the bond window catches it — Dallas County hands it back with "this isn't a Dallas County charge," and the bond gets rewritten. Annoying, but fixable.
- On a **transfer bond** there is no catch. The transfer agents posting for us don't call in discrepancies, and the receipts that come back from the insurance company aren't practically reviewable. On a transfer bond, your intake IS the safety net.

## The Stakes

Even two to five of these a month means two to five bond forfeitures and two to five angry customers hearing "you have court this morning" with no warning. The bond amount is real money — when it goes wrong, we write a check for it.

ia-back-in-jail.title: Back-in-Jail Events — Search First, Mark Every File
ia-back-in-jail.body:
## Never Intake Blind

No intake happens without searching the person in our system first. The caller usually won't announce "he's already on bond with you" — the search is how you find out.

## When the Search Finds Them

Figure out what you're looking at:

- **Previous defendant** — the case is discharged and that file is closed. Note it and move on.
- **Current defendant** — he's on bond with us right now and he's back in jail. That's a **back-in-jail event**, and it must be marked on **every open file he has**, not just the newest one. One defendant recently had three open files — all three needed the event.

Use the linked-files feature (top right corner, next to the face icon) — it shows every file the person has open, tagged together.

## What's Automated and What Isn't

The 17.16 back-in-jail report catches defendants who land back in **Dallas, Collin, or Kaufman County** — one button creates the new intake and the back-in-jail event. For every other jail (Ellis County, Denton, Garland city jail, and the rest), the events must be made **manually**. If you don't make them, nobody does.

ia-case-numbers.title: Case & Warrant Numbers Differ by County
ia-case-numbers.body:
Every North Texas county styles its numbers differently — assuming they all work like Dallas will burn you.

- Most counties' case numbers embed **the year and the court**.
- Some counties skip that format entirely and run a straight seven-digit sequence — just the next number available in the DA's office.
- **Ellis County issues a separate warrant number.** A defendant who misses court does NOT get a warrant under the case number he missed on — the warrant has its own number. You have to call and get it.

The rule that always works: when a warrant is involved, **call and ask for the warrant number** instead of copying whatever number the screen shows.

ia-verify-gracefully.title: Double-Check, Listen, and Stay Graceful
ia-verify-gracefully.body:
## Listen to the Family

When a cosigner says "that's not an Ellis County case — that's out of Dallas," take it seriously. She may have bonded him out on that exact case before — she often knows. On one bond, the mom said exactly that to the underwriter; the information never got forwarded, the closer never asked for clarification, and we posted the wrong county.

- **Underwriters:** forward what the family tells you, even if it contradicts the file.
- **Closers:** double-check what you're about to have posted.

## Everyone Has New People

County clerks and jail staff are learning too — a new clerk might hand back your original without file-stamping it. When you know exactly what you need, you can push back politely: "Are you sure about that?" We work with these people every day — don't make enemies, but don't accept wrong answers either.

Asking the right question pays off. On a recent charge nobody was sure was family violence, one call to the county got them to pull the PC affidavit, see that nothing supported family violence, and release the hold on the spot.

## Own It With the Customer

The court team is only as good as the intake behind them. When the county's wrong and a court date surfaces at the last minute, whoever's on the phone takes the blame and gets the customer to court — no excuses, nobody thrown under the bus. The way to spare everyone that call is to get it right the first time.

q-epros-quote-build.title: Quote Build in ePros — Every Fee, Line by Line
q-epros-quote-build.body:
How to manually quote a bond in ePros, and what every line item is.

## The Mechanics

1. Use the drop-down on the **Quote tab**.
2. Select **Add Fee**.
3. For each fee, select **Save & Add Another** until the quote is complete.

## The Fee Stack

- **Premium** — 10% of the bond, UNLESS the bond is under $2,500. Under $2,500, use the flat tiers: $500–$600 bond = $150 · $600–$800 = $175 · $800–$1,000 = $190 · $1,100–$1,500 = $210.
- **State fee** — $15
- **Admin** — $10
- **Research** — $5
- **Posting fee** — 3% of the bond, unless it is under $2,500.
- **Miscellaneous fee** — $0, UNLESS it's a risk-fee case (IB, PV, ATGOB, FTA) or a geo fee applies — check the geo and risk fee sheet.
- **Fax fee** — $0

## Posting Fee Math

(Bond amount) × 0.03 = posting fee.

- $8,000 bond → $8,000 × 0.03 = $240
- $45,000 bond → $45,000 × 0.03 = $1,350
- $60,000 bond → $60,000 × 0.03 = $1,800

q-risk-fee-spotting.title: Risk Fees — Amounts & How to Spot Them
q-risk-fee-spotting.body:
## What Counts as a Risk Fee

BF (bond forfeiture) · ATGOB (affidavit to go off bond) · FTA (fail to appear) · 17.16 · IB (insufficient bond) · PV (probation violation) · MTR (motion to revoke)

## The Amount

**5% of the bond — $150 minimum, $1,500 maximum.** Anything over a $30,000 bond caps at the $1,500 max. It goes under **6-Miscellaneous Fee** in ePros.

- Bond set at $25,000 → 5% = $1,250
- Bond set at $1,000 → 5% = $50, but the minimum is $150 — so it's $150

## How to Catch One

If the case is **not from this year**, that's your trigger:

1. Ask the jailer: is it a PV? An IB?
2. If they don't know (which is most likely), ask the **caller**: "Are they on bond? Are they on probation?" They will most likely know and tell you everything.
3. Or look it up on **Odyssey**.

Catch it up front and you won't miss a risk fee — and won't hear about it from the closer.

xfr-bankers-portal.title: Posting a Transfer Bond in the Bankers Portal
xfr-bankers-portal.body:
The full walkthrough, from request to accepted quote. You'll work from the **"OK to Post"** — a closer gives you this.

## Create the Request

5. Create the request.

## Before You Accept the Quote

The status line shows how many pending quotes you have. **Before accepting, refer back to the Transfer Fee Sheet to see which sister company we use** — we already have a relationship with them. If the quoting agent is different, **make a note on the "OK to Post" AND in the note section in ePros.**

1. Fill out the blanks from the OK to Post: first & last name, DOB, booking number, race, gender.

3. **Ellis County asks for a lot more** — height, weight, eye color, hair color, driver's license number, etc. Don't freak out: it's all on the Ellis County jail website inmate detail page.
4. **Next of Kin** — use Cosigner 1 and add their name, phone number, and address.
5. Accept the quote.

## After You Accept

- Write on the OK to Post **what time you accepted the quote and which bail bonds company we used**. Also log it in the physical Transfer Bond binder.
- **Be on the lookout for the power numbers.** Once you get them, write them in the binder and on the OK to Post, and give it to an underwriter.

roe-rules.title: Rules of Engagement — Account Ownership
roe-rules.body:
Who gets credit for an account, and when ownership moves. These rules protect the work that happens on the initial sales call.

## The Rules

- **Appointments must be specific.** Every appointment must include a specific date, time, and location.
- **Document the opportunity.** The opportunity must include notes from the sales rep giving a high-level overview of the conversation and relevant details.
- **Missed appointments.** If an appointment is missed, another rep reschedules it, and the cosigner comes into the office — **ownership remains with the original sales rep**.
- **Multiple callers.** When there are multiple callers on an account, credit goes to the rep who **sets the appointment with a specific date, time, and location AND whose cosigner attends**.
- **Given/VIP deals.** For any deal that is given, including a VIP deal, the **first rep to assist** with the account receives credit. One credited rep per account. Maximum payout on these deals is $50 per $100,000.
- **Account ownership.** Reps should **never be removed or eliminated from an account**. Unauthorized removal of a rep from an account may result in disciplinary action.

## The Spirit of It

The work on the initial call matters: building rapport, gathering quality information, answering questions, and establishing trust. If a rep built rapport with a client or indemnitor and got quality information on the first conversation, that effort is respected — simply making a follow-up call because an appointment was missed or rescheduled does **not** automatically transfer ownership.

Each situation gets evaluated on its circumstances. The goal is to recognize the rep who invested the time to build the relationship while making sure every client gets excellent service. We are one team — support one another, don't compete over accounts.

terms-abbrev.title: Everyday Abbreviations
terms-abbrev.body:
The shorthand you'll see in ePros, on jail screens, and around the floor.

- **IB** — Insufficient Bond
- **ATGOB** — Affidavit To Go Off Bond
- **PV** — Probation Violation
- **BF** — Bond Forfeiture
- **MTR** — Motion To Revoke
- **LS** — Lew Sterrett (Dallas County Jail)
- **NC** — NotiCourt subscription ($15 monthly)
- **BIJ** — Back In Jail
- **FMA** — Floor Manager Approval
- **NYA** — Not Yet Arraigned
- **NBA** — No Bond Allowed
- **NFBI / NBI** — Not Fully Booked In
- **XFR** — Transfer
- **17.16** — Insufficient Bond (the surety filing made at the jail)
- **FTA** — Fail To Appear
- **PR Bond** — Personal Recognizance
- **ELM** — Electronic Leg Monitor (ankle monitor)
- **CS / COS** — Cosigner
- **DEF** — Defendant

For the warrant types and what they mean for pricing, see Warrant Types — BF, ATGOB, FTA, IB, PV.
